analysis.one_liner: Ends the federal tax deduction employers get for anti-union campaigns and makes them report that spending.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote: introduced with 29 Democratic-allied cosponsors in March 2023, it sat in the Senate Finance Committee until the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current tax law, a company can deduct what it spends on persuading its own workers not to join a union — consultants, lawyers, and mandatory meetings — so ordinary taxpayers effectively help cover the bill for anti-union campaigns. This bill would deny that deduction and require employers to report their anti-union spending and related activities. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never moved again before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers deciding whether to form a union, who would face fewer employer-funded persuasion campaigns in mandatory meetings, and taxpayers generally, who would stop footing part of the cost through the tax code. Unions organizing new workplaces would face a fairer playing field.

how_it_helps.text: The bill denies employers a tax deduction for expenditures made to influence their own employees about labor organizations, union elections, labor disputes, and collective bargaining [S2][S3].

It treats as non-deductible amounts tied to captive-audience meetings and trainings where unions are discussed, and the costs of actions that result in an unfair labor practice charge or settlement under the National Labor Relations Act [S3].

The bill's findings cite Economic Policy Institute research that employers were charged with unfair labor practices in roughly 4 of 10 union elections in 2016-2017, and that companies spent about $340 million per year on outside consultants to sway workers' opinions about union activity [S3].

It creates a new reporting requirement: employers must disclose the dates, amounts, and nature of covered anti-union spending on their tax returns, with penalties starting at the greater of $10,000 or $1,000 per full-time employee and rising for continued failures, capped at $100,000 [S3].

It exempts ordinary channels of workplace dialogue: direct bargaining with a certified union representative, shareholder communications, voluntary union recognition, legally required postings, and labor-management committees under an existing contract [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers that run anti-union campaigns — mostly large corporations and their union-avoidance consultants — would lose the tax write-off and face new reporting and penalty obligations. Some employers argue the tax penalty would chill legitimate workplace communication.

drawbacks.text: The covered-spending definition is broad: it sweeps in wages and general administrative costs connected to any meeting or training where labor organizations are discussed, and to any conduct that produces an NLRB complaint or settlement — which employers and business groups argue could penalize or chill routine workplace communication about unions [S3].

Penalties are substantial — the greater of $10,000 or $1,000 per full-time employee, escalating up to $100,000 for continued failure to report — which critics of compelled disclosure of employer speech view as a constitutional and administrative burden [S3].

Ending the deduction raises money from employers rather than directly protecting any worker: a company determined to run an anti-union campaign would still be free to do so, just at full cost [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change is modest but real: it removes a taxpayer subsidy for employer campaigns against unionization while leaving the campaigns themselves legal, and it carves out legitimate bargaining and legal-posting costs. The trade-off is a broad spending definition and steep reporting penalties that employers could face even in gray areas, and the bill does nothing to stop the underlying conduct. On balance it shifts power modestly toward workers at a compliance cost to employers.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate introduced the bill and referred it to the Finance Committee, which never took it up, so it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Robert Casey of Pennsylvania introduced the bill on March 9, 2023, with 29 cosponsors from the Democratic caucus [S1][S4].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance — the sole action recorded for the bill's entire two-year lifespan [S5].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote was ever recorded, and the bill expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that fund anti-union campaigns keep their tax deduction and face no reporting requirement, and the union-avoidance consulting industry keeps a tax-subsidized market. Workers deciding whether to organize are no better off than before.

for.name: Sen. Robert Casey Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 29 cosponsors from his party's caucus.

for.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, but as committee chair never scheduled a markup or hearing; the Finance Committee recorded no action on the bill in nearly two years.

for.name: Senate Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support, enough to show caucus-level backing but short of the 60 votes generally needed to advance most legislation on the Senate floor.

sides.party_line_note: All 29 cosponsors were from the Democratic caucus (28 Democrats and 1 Independent), no Republican signed on, and the bill drew no action from the committee where it sat [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Union-avoidance consultants and anti-union law firms
industries.note: The bill's findings cite roughly $340 million a year in employer spending on outside consultants to sway workers against unions; ending the deduction makes that work costlier for clients, and new reporting requirements would make these campaigns public.

industries.industry: Employers that run anti-union campaigns (large corporations)
industries.note: They would pay full price for persuasion campaigns previously written off against taxes, and would owe reporting penalties for failures. Their interest in continuing tax-subsidized anti-union campaigns runs against workers' organizing rights.

industries.industry: Labor unions and workers seeking to organize
industries.note: Union elections would be contested with less employer-funded pressure in mandatory meetings, and the consulting industry's role would shrink rather than become a regulated gatekeeper.
